Friday, 24 December. The flat on rue d’Austerlitz. Around the table: Ioana (almost seven months pregnant), Julien, Hélène, Madame Bernard, Radu and Lucia. On the piano, the little Christmas tree. Victor is asleep underneath it.
Before we serve the Yule log, Ioana and I have some news to tell you.
Again? Last time it was a baby! What will it be this time? Twins?
(laughing) No, Radu. Yesterday we had the last scan. And now we know. It’s a girl.
A girl! I knew it! I’ve known since July. I told Hélène, didn’t I?
You did tell me, Odile. But in September you also said twins.
And the name? Have you already chosen it?
Almost. But before we say it, we’d like to ask someone something. Hélène…
In Iași, my grandmother told us: “Before you choose, ask Hélène.” If you agree, we’d like to call her Rose-Hélène. Rose, like Julien’s grandmother. And Hélène, like you.
(a long silence, then in a trembling voice) For sixty-five years I thought my name would disappear with me. I don’t know what to say…
Say yes, Hélène. For once, don’t think about it.
Yes. Yes, of course. Thank you… Thank you both.
Rose-Hélène Moreau… That’s pretty. But I’m going to call her “Rozi”. The uncle decides, doesn’t he?
What if we listened to Julien’s lullaby? He told me he finished it last night.
(he gets up and goes to the piano) It’s called “For Rose-Hélène”. I began it in July, the day I heard the news. I finished it the day we found out it was a girl.
(softly, as Julien begins to play) Once upon a time… there was a little girl who hadn’t been born yet, and who already had a whole family waiting for her.
had … it (“je l’avais dit” = I had said it)
two (“à vous deux” = to you both)
had … it (“il l’avait finie” = he had finished it)
was (“il était une fois” = once upon a time)
“Eel fü”: passé simple of “être”. You’ll read it very often in books.
“Eel vay-kür”: -urent is read “ür”, the -ent is silent. “Ils vécurent heureux” = the ending of fairy tales.
“Ee-lay-tay-tün-fwa”: linked, with liaison on t. The beginning of every French fairy tale.
“Ray-vay-yõ”: the big dinner on Christmas Eve (24 December) or New Year’s Eve (31 December).
“Büsh”: the Yule log, a rolled cake in the shape of a log.
1. The passé simple: the tense of books

In books, fairy tales, novels and history articles, the French use the PASSÉ SIMPLE for the past instead of the passé composé. It’s hardly ever used in speech. English has nothing like it — the passé simple simply corresponds to the English past (“he left”, “she said”), but only in writing.
At A2 and B1 you only need to RECOGNISE it when you read. You don’t need to use it. The imparfait stays the same in books (for the setting); only the passé composé becomes the passé simple.
You’ll almost always see it in the third person (il, elle, ils, elles). Here are the endings:
Watch out for traps: “il dit” can be present (he says) or passé simple (he said). “Il fit” has nothing to do with fitness! It means “he did / made”.
Ils vécurent heureux et eurent beaucoup d’enfants.
They lived happily ever after and had many children.

The classic French fairy tales are by Charles Perrault (1697): “Cendrillon” (Cinderella), “La Belle au bois dormant” (Sleeping Beauty), “Le Petit Chaperon rouge” (Little Red Riding Hood). They’re an excellent first step into literature!

When did Julien start the lullaby?
Once upon a time there was a little girl…

When Julien played the last notes of the lullaby, nobody spoke for a long time. Outside, night had long since fallen. The lights of the Christmas tree were reflected in the window, and in the distance you could hear the cathedral bells announcing midnight mass.
Suddenly Ioana put her hand on her belly. She went very pale, then very red. “Julien… She moved. For the first time. During the lullaby.”
Julien rushed over to her. He put his hand next to Ioana’s. They waited. Nothing. Then, a few seconds later, a tiny little kick, very light, like a butterfly gently knocking at a door.

“She likes your music,” Ioana whispered. Julien couldn’t speak any more. Madame Bernard, who had been a doctor for forty years and had felt hundreds of babies move, discreetly wiped her eyes with her napkin.

“Play it again, Julien,” Hélène asked. “If she moves again, it means she really is a musician.” Julien played the lullaby again. And Rose-Hélène moved again, twice, at exactly the same moment in the melody. The whole table applauded.
“I told you so,” declared Radu, very proud. “She’ll be a pianist, like her father. But she’ll speak Romanian with me. And she’ll love sarmale.”

At about eleven, Lucia got up to look out of the window. She let out a little cry. “Come and see! It’s snowing!” Everyone came over. Big white flakes were falling slowly on rue d’Austerlitz, on the roofs of Croix-Rousse, on the darkened window of Sophie’s bakery.
“It hasn’t snowed in Lyon at Christmas for twelve years,” said Madame Bernard. Hélène came slowly over to the window with her stick. She looked at the snow for a long time, with a strange smile.

“The last time I saw it snow on Christmas Eve in Lyon,” she said softly, “was in 1961. Henri had come to my parents’ house for the first time. He had brought an orange for my mother and a book for my father. We had gone out into the street, in the snow, and he had said to me: ‘Next year, I’ll write you a waltz.’”

She turned to Ioana and Julien. “And he wrote it. And sixty-five years later, you played it for a little girl who will bear my name. I think he’s watching us tonight. With Rose, and with all those we have loved.”

Nobody answered. There was nothing to say. Madame Bernard took Hélène’s hand. Radu took Lucia’s hand. Julien put his arm around Ioana’s shoulders. And all six of them stayed at the window, watching the snow fall, while Victor slept under the Christmas tree.

At midnight, Ioana’s phone rang. It was a video call from Iași. On the screen was the whole family: Elena, Dan, the grandmother, and even the cousin with the țuică, who was already raising his glass. “Crăciun fericit! Joyeux Noël!” they all shouted together.

Ioana showed them the snow through the window. Then she told them it was a girl, and that she would be called Rose-Hélène. The grandmother put her hands on her heart. Then she said something in Romanian, and this time Ioana translated it for everyone: “She says she’ll come in March. By coach. With twenty kilos of sarmale.”

Before leaving, Hélène took a big, very old yellow envelope out of her bag. Ioana recognised it at once: it was the envelope they had found in the piano two years earlier, on the day of the move. Inside was the original score of the waltz, handwritten by Henri in 1962.
“I’ve kept it for sixty-five years,” said Hélène. “Now I’d like it to belong to Rose-Hélène. When she’s grown up, you’ll tell her the story. And maybe one day she’ll play it for someone she loves.”

Madame Bernard took out a little parcel too. It was a framed photo: Henri, young, on his ship, laughing. “For her bedroom,” she explained. “So that she knows the face of the man who wrote her first music.” She and Hélène smiled at each other, like two sisters.
Later, when everyone had gone, Ioana opened the baby’s diary. She reread the first page, from 22 July. Then she wrote a new page, the last of the year:

“My little Rose-Hélène, tonight you moved for the first time, while your daddy was playing your lullaby. It was snowing on Lyon. You won’t remember it, but I will never forget it. Two years ago, I came to this city with a suitcase and a dictionary. I didn’t know anyone. Today I have a family, two countries, and you.”

“One day, when you’re grown up, I’ll tell you the whole story. The story of a piano, a waltz and a promise. It begins like fairy tales: once upon a time… But it doesn’t end. Because now, you’re the one who will write it.”

The next morning, Christmas Day, the snow still covered the whole of Croix-Rousse. In the letterbox, Ioana found a postcard from Corsica. There were only a few words, written in a shaky hand: “Merry Christmas to the lovers of Lyon. Come and introduce me to the baby in the spring. Antoine.”

Down below, in front of the bakery, Sophie was clearing the snow with a shovel. When she saw Ioana at the window, she held up a paper bag. “Christmas croissants! Free for the mum-to-be!” And in the street, under the snowflakes, Radu and Lucia were throwing snowballs at each other, laughing like children.

Julien came over to the window, a cup of tea in his hand. He looked at the white street, the bakery, the children playing, the piano behind him. He thought of Henri, of Marcel and Rose, of all those who were no longer there. Then he put his hand on Ioana’s belly and felt a little kick. “Merry Christmas, Rose-Hélène,” he whispered.

Hélène wrote a fairy tale for Rose-Hélène and read it on Christmas Eve. Watch out for the passé simple! Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Le pianiste et la jeune fille
Once upon a time, in a city between two rivers, there was a girl who loved to laugh and a young man who played the piano.
One spring Thursday, the young man wrote a waltz for the girl. He gave it to her with a little green ring and promised her he would come back.

But a war broke out, far away, on the other side of the sea. The young man left. When he came back, his hand was wounded, and he could no longer play. So he was ashamed, and he never came back to the city.
The girl waited a long time. Then she became an old lady. She kept the waltz in a piano, and the ring in a drawer, for sixty years.
One day, a young musician bought the old piano. A young architect from a faraway country found the waltz. And together, they played it again.
The old lady gave them the ring. They were married on a Monday in May, and the whole city danced the waltz of the young man who had never come back.

And one winter’s day, they told the old lady that a little girl was going to be born, and that she would bear her name. Then the old lady understood that promises are always kept in the end. You just have to be patient. The End.

had not … (“qui n’était jamais revenu” = who had never come back)
was going to (“allait naître” = was going to be born)
end up (“finissent par être” = end up being)
